Webshare is a good NetNut replacement for small and mid-size developer teams: static ISP proxies start at $6 for 20 IPs, rotating residential costs $27.50 for 10 GB and $225 for 100 GB, and SOCKS5, ASN selection and US city and ZIP targeting are included. Before moving high-volume NetNut workloads, check the default 500-request concurrency limit and remember that monthly bandwidth resets every 30 days. Webshare and NetNut both sold static ISP and rotating residential proxies, so Webshare is a natural candidate for former NetNut customers since the FBI seized NetNut's domains in July 2026. Webshare is cheaper, fully self-service and developer-friendly, with an 80M+ advertised residential pool and a free datacenter plan. It also has limits worth knowing before you migrate, such as monthly bandwidth resets and a default concurrency cap. This page covers both.
What happened to NetNut?

On July 2, 2026, the FBI, working with IRS Criminal Investigation, Google, Lumen and the Shadowserver Foundation, seized hundreds of domains tied to NetNut, the residential proxy service owned by Nasdaq-listed Alarum Technologies. Google's Threat Intelligence Group said NetNut's exit-node pool overlapped with Popa, a botnet it estimated at about two million consumer devices, many of them smart TVs and streaming boxes. Alarum disputes the botnet label and said it would cooperate with law enforcement, but netnut.com and, within days, netnut.io displayed federal seizure notices. As of October 2026 the service is not something you can responsibly buy or rely on.

blocks.text: Webshare in 2026: what you get

Webshare is the self-service favourite of solo developers. It gives away 10 shared datacenter proxies with 1 GB a month forever, sells paid datacenter lists from $2.99 for 100 proxies, and offers static ISP and rotating residential networks with a clean dashboard and good API. Its rotating residential pool is listed at 80M+ IPs in 195 countries, with sticky sessions from one minute to 24 hours. The main catch is that monthly bandwidth resets every 30 days and does not roll over.

Webshare is built for developers who want to configure everything themselves. Pricing is transparent, the free datacenter plan makes it easy to test integrations, and paid plans scale smoothly from tiny to large. Its residential network advertises 80M+ IPs across 195 countries. It does not sell mobile proxies or a broad scraping API, and paid plans start with an account-wide limit of 500 concurrent requests.

Strengths: Permanent free datacenter plan for testing; Low, transparent residential pricing; Excellent dashboard and API; Sticky sessions up to 24 hours. Weak spots: Bandwidth resets monthly with no rollover; No mobile proxies; 500-request default concurrency limit.
What NetNut offered, and how Webshare compares

Before the seizure, NetNut was best known for ISP-sourced static residential proxies and a fast rotating residential network aimed at scraping, ad verification and brand-protection teams. Its residential rates generally ran from about $1.87 to $3.53 per GB on larger plans, with higher effective prices on entry plans. Webshare covers much of the same ground: datacenter proxy servers, static residential (isp) sit alongside its residential network, which advertises 80M+ IPs in 195 countries.
What former NetNut customers need, and whether Webshare
delivers

Most NetNut accounts were built around three things: static ISP IPs for long-lived sessions, rotating residential traffic with US state and city targeting, and high concurrency for scraping. On static ISP-style IPs, Webshare's answer is yes; its other products are datacenter proxy servers, static residential (ISP). On rotating residential targeting, Webshare offers country, plus state, city or ZIP (US) or ASN in 195 countries, with rotating or sticky from 1 minute to 24 hours. On billing, Webshare uses monthly or yearly subscription, and unused traffic is handled as follows: allowance resets every 30 days; no rollover. Map each of your old NetNut zones to one of these before you migrate, so nothing breaks on the day you switch.
Webshare pricing

Webshare's rotating residential plans cost $3.50 for 1 GB, $27.50 for 10 GB, $65 for 25 GB, $225 for 100 GB and $875 for 500 GB per month, falling to $1.40/GB at 3 TB. Yearly billing is about 30% cheaper but is paid upfront for a 360-day term. Unused bandwidth resets every 30 days.

Quick cost check for Webshare: 10 GB comes to $27.50 (10 GB monthly, $2.75/GB), and 100 GB comes to $225 (100 GB monthly, $2.25/GB). NetNut's larger plans used to run about $1.87-$3.53/GB, so compare against what you actually paid rather than NetNut's headline rate.
How to migrate from NetNut to Webshare
1. Export your NetNut usage history and list the countries, cities and session types you actually used, so you can map them to Webshare's targeting (country, plus state, city or ZIP (US) or ASN).

2. Test before you commit. Webshare's testing option: 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial. Run your real targets for a day on the smallest purchase before moving production traffic.
3. Swap the gateway host and credentials in your scraper or browser profiles. Webshare supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5.
4. Compare success rate, response time and cost per successful request against your old NetNut baseline, then move traffic over in stages.
5. Remove any NetNut SDKs, browser extensions or endpoints from your systems, and rotate any credentials that were stored alongside them.
Where Webshare fits best
General web scraping: strong fit. Why: low prices and a developer-friendly API.
SERP and rank tracking: workable. Why: fine for light rank tracking.
Social media and multi-account management: strong fit. Why: 24-hour sticky sessions and cheap static ISP IPs.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: workable. Why: good for US work with ZIP targeting, thinner elsewhere.
Ad verification and geo-testing: weak fit. Why: no mobile network and limited selector combinations.
Tight budgets: strong fit. Why: free tier plus some of the lowest per-GB rates here.
Protocols and sessions

Webshare supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5 and offers rotating or sticky from 1 minute to 24 hours. Targeting covers country, plus state, city or ZIP (US) or ASN across 195 countries. Like NetNut's residential gateway, it works through a single backconnect endpoint with location and session options passed in the username, plus IP whitelisting.
How to vet a residential proxy provider after NetNut

NetNut's customers did not choose to route traffic through a botnet; they bought what looked like a standard enterprise service. The lesson is to check sourcing before you buy, not after. Whichever provider replaces NetNut for you, Webshare included, run through these checks:
How are residential IPs sourced? Look for an opt-in SDK or app programme with clear user
consent and compensation, and ask which partner apps are involved.
Does the provider publish an ethics or sourcing policy, and has it been audited or certified (for
example AppEsteem or ISO 27001)?
What KYC does the provider apply to customers, and which target categories are restricted?
Strict onboarding is a good sign, not an inconvenience.
How does it handle abuse reports, and is there a named legal entity and jurisdiction behind the
service?
Can you get contractual assurances, such as a data-processing agreement, if your compliance
team needs them?
Bottom line

NetNut is no longer a provider you can plan around, so the real decision is which network replaces it. Webshare is strongest for solo developers and small teams and budget scraping with predictable monthly volume, starts at $3.50 for 1 GB per month, and offers 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial. Test it on your own targets for a day, compare cost per successful request with your old NetNut baseline, and move production traffic in stages.
